While a trade war between Canada and the United States has seen Carney go hunting for new geopolitical partners, an over-reliance on American companies – especially for defence – has also given Canada pause.
Last week, Elon Musk throttled the speeds of Starlink and Starshield over Ukraine in mid-October, severely disrupting Ukrainian military and defense operations.

Carney has repeatedly raised the concern that Canada’s defense technologies could be at the whim of political actors or companies with opposing interests. Musk, a dual Canadian citizen, is a critic of Canada’s governing Liberal party and has advocated for provinces to separate.

Carney pointed to a planned merger between the Canadian artificial intelligence company Cohere Inc and Germany’s Aleph Alpha GmbH as a step to lessening reliance on American AI giants. The tie-up will see the newly formed company have dual headquarters in Berlin and Toronto, and Canada’s federal government has announced a stake in Cohere worth up to C$1.6bn.
“We are not waiting for the future of AI to be decided somewhere else by those we don’t know, or by whom we don’t trust,” Carney said on Thursday.
Brussels and Ottawa also announced an agreement on Friday that would bringing Canada into Europe’s supercomputing network, giving Canadian access to European machines to train AI models.

In addition to lofty promises of helping to reshape the global order, or giving safe harbour to like-minded nations looking to weather uncertainty, Canadian and EU leaders also pitched their new, deeper relationship as one that addressed key sources of anxiety for residents, including the cost of living.

“When trade becomes a tool of economic pressure, it’s the families that pay the price, from the supermarket shelf to the cost of a new car,” Von der Leyen said, noting that previously trusted trusted suppliers of energy, critical minerals or semiconductors “are increasingly turned into instruments of pressure”.
“More competition, more choice,” Carney said earlier in the day, suggesting the alliance could find ways to build certainty around supply chains and “withstand shocks, together”.

The leaders once again brought up the prospect of Canada becoming an associate member. The designation is uncharted territory, said Von der Leyen, who added: “We have the ambition, trust, and creativity to shape it together.
“This [associate membership] is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength.”

While the leaders committed to the idea of associate membership, they said a clearer scope of the role would come at a 2027 summit. Some EU members had bristled at the idea of Canada being given a legally meaningless designation that they fear confuses other nations looking for membership. Germany and other states had worked behind the scenes to remove the phrase from a draft of the summit statement. But Von der Leyen, who first floated the term, and Carney both again referred to “associate membership” at the summit.

European Council president Antonio Costa, meanwhile, said earlier that Canada was “by far the most European of the non-European countries”, a sentiment that reflected a belief that despite geography, there was a collective sense of shared values.
Costa said the two sides would pursue “the most closer, the most deepest, the most stronger association ever between European Union and a non-European country”.

Still, the mere fact of the summit has caused friction in the province of Quebec, where the separatist Parti Québécois was recently elected to a minority government. The premier, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, skipped the event after Ottawa’s refusal to let him speak publicly at it.

“The federal government would have us believe that the premier of Quebec being granted permission to serve shrimp cocktails at a reception constitutes an acceptable and sufficient form of influence for representing Quebec’s interests,” St-Pierre Plamondon wrote in a social media post earlier in the week.

He said an invitation to sit at the head table was the federal government asking Quebec “to get back in line, with the vassalization and invisibilization of Quebec which that implies, in exchange for obtaining better seats to watch the party”.

articles.title: Roy Moxham obituary
articles.summary: Other lives: Author of The Great Hedge of India who began his career working on a tea plantation in Africa
body: My uncle Roy Moxham, who has died aged 86, was a former tea plantation supervisor who in later life turned his hand to writing about tea and about India, a country he visited many times on extended trips.

His most successful book was The Great Hedge of India (2001), which was published not just in English but in multiple Indian languages. The hedge of the title, which was four metres high and 2.5m wide, was made of thorny shrubs and stretched 2,500 miles across British India to form a customs line guarded by 12,000 men on behalf of the East India Company.

Following independence in 1947 it all but disappeared, but Roy spent many of his visits to the country looking for vestiges, eventually finding a small surviving section. He cut a branch from it, and it is now in the possession of his brother John (my father), kept safely in his study.

Roy’s other books included A Brief History of Tea (2003), an authoritative account of the complex political and horticultural history of tea, and Outlaw (2010), which looked at the life of India’s “bandit queen” and politician Phoolan Devi, drawing on Roy’s friendship with her before her assassination in 2001. His last book, The Theft of India (2015), documented the rivalry between European colonial powers and the impact this had on Indians themselves.

Roy was born in Evesham, Worcestershire, to Marie (known as Min, nee Bland) and Wilson Moxham. Wilson, a baker, died when Roy was 11, after which Min, a shop worker, raised her three sons under straitened circumstances, often taking in lodgers to make ends meet.

After leaving Prince Henry’s grammar school in Evesham in the early 1960s, Roy put an advert in the Times newspaper that read: “Young man, good A-levels, seeks opportunity in Africa in tobacco or tea.” He received a reply offering him a job on a tea plantation in the British colony of Nyasaland (now Malawi), where, despite his youth, he became a supervisor in charge of 1,000 female tea pickers. Later he switched to selling agricultural machinery across east Africa, particularly in Kenya. In the mid-70s, after 13 years in Africa he returned to the UK, where he opened a gallery in Covent Garden, London, selling African art.

Following a period of squatting in Covent Garden, Roy became an early and longstanding member of the Seven Dials Housing Co-operative, living in one of their properties in that area for most of the rest of his life.

In 1978 he changed direction by studying book and paper conservation at Camberwell College of Arts, after which he worked as a conservator at the Canterbury Cathedral Archive, then at Senate House Library, University of London, where he remained until 2005.

While working, Roy had begun travelling regularly to India from 1992 onwards, and it was on those journeys that he began his three-year search for the Great Hedge. The book was hugely successful, often referenced by historians, writers and artists, and even inspired a Horrible Histories sketch.

After retiring in 2005, Roy lived in India for a number of months each year. His book about Devi, a champion of the Indian poor, came about after he wrote to her when she was in prison. When she was released they arranged a meeting, and became great friends.
Roy is survived by his two brothers, John and Jim, a nephew, three nieces and me.

articles.title: How crypto hacking funds isolated North Korea’s nuclear programme
articles.summary: Cryptocurrency theft is estimated to generate half of the country’s foreign currency income
body: North Korea plays by its own rules. The isolated, secretive and autocratic country is largely cut off from the world’s economic system – but when it comes to generating foreign earnings it relies on some of the world’s most sophisticated hacking.

Experts, such as TRM Labs, quickly attributed the extraordinary $6.3bn (£4.7bn) Binance cryptocurrency theft to TraderTraitor, an elite North Korean hacking unit that has also been known as the Lazarus Group. Though the link may not be proven yet, the pattern of behaviour is familiar.

North Korea has a history of cryptocurrency theft dating back to 2017, focusing on the sector’s relatively lax security controls as a way of stealing money and generating revenues for its military, including its nuclear weapons programme.

Kim Jong-un, its dictatorial ruler, controls a stockpile of about 50 nuclear warheads, and has been supplying troops and weapons to help Russia in its war in Ukraine. But North Korea is also extremely poor: 40% of the population are undernourished according to the UN and nearly one in five of its children are stunted.
Related: North Korea is likely culprit behind $6.3bn crypto hack, ‘largest heist in history’

A UN panel of experts, reporting to the security council, said in the spring of 2024 that it was reviewing “58 suspected cyber-attacks” by North Korea “on cryptocurrency-related companies between 2017 and 2023” worth $3bn.

The panel said the cash was estimated to generate half of North Korea’s foreign currency income. One unnamed country went further with its estimate: the stolen billions fund “40% of the weapons of mass destruction programmes”.

The suspected crypto hacks amounted to as many as 17 in 2023 alone: thefts valued at $750m, and disturbingly, the sums involved are only increasing. The world’s largest previous crypto hack took place in February 2025, when $1.5bn was stolen from the Bybit exchange – the work, the FBI said, of TraderTraitor.

Ciaran Martin, a former head of the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre, argues that North Korea appears to have targeted crypto because traditional banks have developed sophisticated defences that the fast-growing and lightly regulated sector has yet to match.

“Over the last decade, hackers have walked off with nine- or 10-figure sums from crypto hacks on more than 30 occasions. The number of traditional banks who have suffered a loss of more than $100m as a result of a cyber-attack in the same period is zero or one,” Martin said.

North Korea was behind one of the last large cyber thefts on a traditional bank – an attack on Bangladesh Bank in February 2016, where North Korean hackers tried to illicitly move $951m from an account the bank had with the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, taking advantage of time differences between the two.

A piece of luck prevented most of the money from being sent to an intermediate account in the Philippines. The corresponding bank was based on Jupiter Street, which shares its first word with the name of a sanctioned Iranian ship, so most of the transfers were held up. In the end, $81m was stolen.

The isolated state has long been accused of engaging in criminal activities to survive, including the forgery of high-quality $100 bills, known as “supernotes” in the 1990s, and the production and trafficking of crystal meth for export in the 2000s.

The UK has been rarely targeted. In 2019, North Korean hackers did try to take control of cash machines linked to 56 financial institutions to make them pay out sums well in excess of normal. British officials spotted what was afoot, alerted the banks and the hack was quietly suppressed with no media coverage.
Related: How big a deal is the $6.3bn crypto heist, who did it, and are investments safe?

The irony is that the internet in North Korea is severely restricted, with access denied to the general population. Maths and science are pushed at school, however, and at university some of the best students are recruited into hacker groups, such as Lazarus, operating under the auspices of the country’s Reconnaissance General Bureau spy agency.

Hacking is closely tied to the all-powerful state. In December 2014, it emerged, to the embarrassment of Sony Pictures, that film stars Jennifer Lawrence and Amy Adams were paid less than their male counterparts in American Hustle. It was one of thousands of embarrassing emails leaked from the Hollywood studio through a hack.

The attack, by North Korea’s Lazarus Group, was conducted because Sony had funded a film, The Interview: a Seth Rogen comedy that depicted the assassination of Kim Jong-un. Amid the chaos of the revelations, Sony tried to cancel the movie, then had to U-turn on its retreat, releasing it online and to a handful of cinemas, after being criticised for caving in to North Korean pressure.

articles.title: Evacuation of civilians begins in besieged Ukrainian city of Oleshky
articles.summary: Humanitarian convoy brings food and medicine to Russian-held city where people have suffered severe shortages
body: People living in the besieged Russian-held city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine were evacuated on Friday as part of a joint relief operation, the first of its kind in four years and eight months of war.

The city, which lies on the Russian-occupied side of the Dnipro River, opposite Kherson, has suffered months of serious food and medical shortages, leading to warnings of starvation for the few thousand people remaining there, including about 50 children.
The humanitarian convoy, including 25 buses and ambulances, had arrived in the city to deliver food and medicine and evacuate those wishing to leave for Russia or Ukraine.
The localised ceasefire in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region allowed for the roads out of Oleshky to be de-mined, making evacuation possible.

While Ukrainian territory lies just 3 miles (5km) from Oleshky, evacuees will need to travel to the southern Russian city of Anapa and on to Belarus, and then drive across the border into Ukraine’s Chernihiv region.

Davyd Arakhamia, a lawmaker with the Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s Servant of the People party – who was part of the delegation to Oleshky – confirmed the evacuation of some people who were travelling to Anapa.
“From there, they will fly by plane to Belarus, and then travel by bus to their homes,” he said.

Kyrylo Budanov, the head of Ukraine’s presidential office, wrote in an online post: “At this moment, the humanitarian operation is under way in Oleshky.” Budanov is not part of the delegation in Oleshky.
While earlier reports had suggested more than 500 people wanted to move to Ukrainian territory, it was unclear how many people travelled in the convoy.

Kyiv’s delegation reached the city late on Friday morning to prepare for the evacuation, with footage on social media showing tearful residents embracing delegation members as they gathered in heavy rain to wait for the main evacuation convoy to arrive. Several hundred people, mainly older people, have chosen to stay.

Asked if she was packed and ready to leave by a member of the Ukrainian delegation, a woman who identified herself as “Anna” was shown on video saying: “Yes, we are on bus 20, my son is on bus 17. To Ukraine.”

Oleshky’s population has declined to about 2,000 since the star of the war, according to authorities and volunteers, and many of those who stayed have given harrowing accounts of risking their lives travelling along mine-strewn roads to get food and water.
Some say they have survived on a cup of rice or buckwheat a day, sometimes with a tomato, cucumber or wild plants added.

“We’ve been through so much here in these five years,” one woman said in a report broadcast on Ukrainian TV. Another older woman, preparing to evacuate, said: “If we had our health, maybe we’d stay there a bit longer, but that’s it. We just want to be with our children.”
Related: ‘Hell on earth’: last residents eat weeds to survive in Russian-occupied Oleshky
Ksenia Arkhipova, a volunteer who previously lived in Oleshky and remains in contact with people there, said large numbers of Russian military personnel were in the city.

“They are currently checking empty houses and, in some cases, moving into them,” she told the Associated Press. “They are also pressuring local residents to evacuate to Russia, rather than to Ukraine,” she added.
The convoy arrived under a ceasefire in the area, which the US first lady, Melania Trump, claimed to have helped broker – a rare example of cooperation between the warring sides.
On Friday, the Kremlin, however, described it as a special case that was “difficult to extrapolate” to the wider search for a peace settlement.
Oleshky was seized by Russian troops during the first days of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
It has suffered extensive damage and was badly flooded after the destruction of the huge upriver Kakhovka dam in June 2023.

“The problem is that a lot of people are staying,” one woman told Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, who was on the ground to coordinate the operation with his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova.
“I’ve been told that ‌it’s their own choice,” Lubinets replied. “At the very least, we’ll do what we can to ensure that somehow humanitarian aid gets through.”
He added: “This is the first time since 2022 that a ceasefire has been established across such an extensive stretch of the frontline and has been maintained for ​such a significant duration.”

articles.title: Pope Leo votes in US midterms in first known political ballot for any pontiff
articles.summary: US citizen Leo, who has clashed with Donald Trump over several issues, submits his vote by post in Chicago
body: Pope Leo has voted in the US midterm elections – the first time a sitting pontiff is known to have cast a ballot in any political election at any time in history.

Leo, who has clashed with the US president, Donald Trump, over several issues, submitted his vote by post in Chicago, where he was born, the Vatican said on Friday. Leo became the first American leader of the Catholic church last year after the death of Pope Francis.

The Vatican said Leo “has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen, whenever he was eligible to do so”, including in Peru, where he lived for years as a missionary. “The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes,” the statement added.
Related: The US midterm races that will decide control of Congress – mapped
Leo, who before being elected pope was known as Robert Prevost, reportedly made his request for the mail-in ballot on 3 October, registering at an address in New Lenox, Illinois.
That was 10 days before he had surgery to remove a cancerous tumour from his right lung. The pontiff has gradually been resuming activities since being discharged from hospital on 17 October.
The crucial midterm elections are due to be held on 3 November.
Leo and Trump have clashed over the US president’s harsh immigration polices, with the pontiff describing them as “inhuman”.

Earlier this year, Trump lashed out in response to Leo’s criticisms of the US-Israeli war on Iran, calling the pontiff “weak on crime” and “terrible on foreign policy”. The US president also said Leo had only been elected pope because Trump himself was in the White House.
In response to the tirade, Leo said he was “not afraid” of Trump.
Related: ‘A pope who uses his brain’: Vatican locals and visitors take sides in Leo v Trump spat

In his first key address to the US on the eve of the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, Leo praised the country’s history of ⁠welcoming migrants, while urging Americans to live up to the ideals put forward in the ⁠declaration, in what was seen a further rebuke to Trump.

In an interview with the US broadcaster in late July, Leo expressed “great love” for his home country and its core principles of freedom, opportunity and welcoming immigrants but qualified that he just “happens to be American”.

Leo will travel to Latin America in November for an 11-day trip covering 10 cities. Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher, the Holy See’s foreign minister, told reporters at Rome’s foreign press association this week that a papal visit to the US was expected in the “not too distant future”, adding that the outcome of the midterms might influence whether the trip went ahead in 2027 or later.

articles.title: Russian society being ‘systematically crushed’ says Novaya Gazeta as newspaper announces closure
articles.summary: Independent outlet, whose former editor Dmitry Muratov won Nobel prize, cites intolerable pressure from authorities Europe live – latest updates
body: Novaya Gazeta, one of Russia’s best-known independent media outlets, has announced it will permanently close next month. The newspaper, whose former editor-in-chief Dmitry Muratov won the Nobel peace prize in 2021, cited intolerable pressure, including being stripped of its newsroom, its donation platforms and its legal right to publish.
“This is not just our own story; it is the story of a country and a society that are being systematically crushed,” wrote its editor-in-chief, Sergei Sokolov, on the newspaper’s website.

Launched in the 1990s and for many years partly funded by the late Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev, Novaya made its name through dogged, long-form reporting on corruption, rights abuses and social issues. Over the years, six of its journalists have been assassinated, including Anna Politkovskaya, who was gunned down in the stairwell of her Moscow apartment block in 2006.

While Novaya always swam against a tide of repression, the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 made independent reporting almost impossible and decimated the Russian media landscape. Novaya was one of the last critical voices still operating from inside the country.

“For nearly five years of ***, we managed to keep working while being completely encircled by the security services. Now it’s over. We have found ourselves in a ‘kill zone’,” wrote Sokolov. The stars were used in place of the word “war”, as under Russian law, journalists must refer to the war in Ukraine as a “special military operation” or face consequences.

The newspaper’s first response to the invasion was to put out a special bilingual Russian-Ukrainian edition in the days after Vladimir Putin launched the invasion. It described the war as “madness” on its front page. Soon after, the Kremlin implemented draconian new censorship laws, which forced media outlets to publish only the Russian official narrative about the conflict.

“We said it’s not journalism and we’re not going to do that,” said Nadezhda Prusenkova, the head of Novaya’s press service. The newspaper published blank white spaces instead of euphemisms and false information, to provide a visible reminder of the censorship laws.

By the end of March 2022, Novaya decided to stop publishing its print edition altogether, but the threats and pressure only increased. In April that year, Muratov was doused with red paint while on a train, an attack that damaged his eyesight and that US officials say was carried out on the orders of Russian intelligence agencies. In September that year, the newspaper’s official licence was taken away and soon after their website was blocked in Russia.

Novaya’s journalists, long used to operating in a hostile environment, found ways to circumvent the bans. Many left Russia, and a number of exiled former employees set up Novaya Gazeta Europe, a legally distinct outlet. Muratov and a core team stayed behind and continued to publish a series of magazines with a print run of 999 copies, taking advantage of a law that means magazines with under 1,000 copies do not require an official licence. Novaya’s website continued running, too, although the Russian state hit the outlet with various new legal threats.

“The fact Novaya kept working for this four and a half years after everything that happened was a miracle, but it was not just a miracle, it was also the daily choice of people who continued to go to work even when it was very scary,” said Elena Kostyuchenko, a former Novaya journalist who spent 17 years at the newspaper. “Today I feel very inspired by my colleagues, but also very painful and sad for them, and for all of us.”
Related: ​Pragmatic or pointless? Europe’s rift over whether to pick up the phone to Putin

In recent months, Prusenkova said the pressure had become intolerable. In April, the journalist Oleg Roldugin was arrested and charged with “unlawful access to computerised information”. He is under house arrest awaiting trial and last month Sokolov’s home was searched as part of the case.

This month, the newspaper’s landlords informed Novaya staff that they must vacate their longstanding office premises in central Moscow by 9 November. The newsroom has been the hub of the newspaper for decades and houses a memorial museum to Politkovskaya in the former office of the murdered journalist. Prusenkova said the exhibits would be taken down and put into storage, for now.

On top of the eviction notice, all the outlet’s donation platforms have been shut down, leaving the paper without any source of funding. The court case, combined with the eviction and the lack of funds, gave the newspaper no choice but to close, said staff.

“Sometimes it happens that your enemies win. At this moment in time, it seems like they have won, and we have no options left,” said Prusenkova. But she said it was probable Novaya’s journalists would try to find some way to continue their work. “After all, we don’t know how to do anything else,” she said.

articles.title: Cost of living protests to spread to Germany and reignite in France on Halloween
articles.summary: Activists call for people to make their anger known over poor public services including education and housing
body: Street protests sweeping Europe are expected to spread to Germany and reignite in France on Saturday, with police mobilised to stop potential looting and rioting on the fringes of what organisers hope will be peaceful rallies.

Weeks of, at times violent, student demonstrations have rocked Italy, Spain, Portugal, Albania and France, where activists on Halloween have again called for people to make their anger over the cost of living and deficient public services felt across the country.

In Germany, a loose alliance of groups called Gen Z regelt (Gen Z is sorting it) has called for supporters to turn out in more than 30 cities demanding more spending on schools, climate protection and housing, and against any plans to return to mandatory military service.

Alexander Throm, of the ruling conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) parliamentary group, wrote in the Handelsblatt business newspaper: “Scenes like those in France must be prevented at all costs.”
But Felix Banaszak, the co-leader of the opposition Green party, cautioned against attempts to place the youth protests under general suspicion in advance.

“The [CDU’s] rhetoric, which seeks to criminalise these protests pre-emptively and paint them as the work of marauding gangs, may even drive people towards radicalisation,” he told the RND media group.
Berlin’s police chief, Barbara Slowik Meisel, said she would deploy an additional 1,500 officers in the capital, though she had little reason to fear that people or property would come under attack.
“We have no concrete evidence of any coordinated looting operations being planned,” she said.

About 10,000 protesters, mainly pupils, students and their parents, are expected at the Brandenburg Gate on Saturday afternoon, with another smaller gathering planned in the early evening in the Mitte district.
Large rallies have also been called in Cologne, Munich, Frankfurt and Hamburg.

The team behind Gen Z regelt has used social media and its website to call on participants to exercise restraint: “Our protest is peaceful, without exception. Violence goes against everything we stand for. Only through peaceful means can we achieve something together.”
By Friday, more than 160,000 people had registered on the website saying they planned to attend the protests.

The federal pupils’ conference, a youth political lobbying group, has distanced itself from Saturday’s demonstrations, saying the initiative’s “unclear” organisational structure made the events unpredictable.
It plans to hold a separate protest in Berlin on 20 November that will include teachers and other youth movements focused on the marked decline in German school performance.

In France, the interior minister, Laurent ⁠Nuñez, said Saturday looked like “a very high risk” day, adding that 70,000 police and gendarmes, including elite units, would be deployed in an effort to quell violence on the sidelines of the new wave of protests.

Nuñez said late on Thursday that radical groups had called on social media for violent Halloween gatherings and that the biggest threat to public order would probably come after mainstream cost-of-living demonstrations had officially ended.

“We are seeing many calls from the labour movement, the radicalised far left and certain radicalised gilets jaunes [yellow vests], urging people to attend rallies on public streets starting at 8pm in many cities ‌across France,” he said.

The calls were “accompanied by various messages which are quite radical”, Nuñez added, including some demanding “revolution”. He said authorities would “tolerate zero excesses” and promised an “extremely firm” security response.

Measures introduced last weekend to protect shops would be reinforced, Nuñez said, and while peaceful demonstrations would be authorised, most would not be permitted “in city centres, where there is a risk of public disorder”.

It is unclear what will happen in Paris. Two separate marches planned by unions and gilets jaunes through the city centre have been banned. Instead, police have authorised a single march in the far south-east. Both sets of organisers are challenging the decision to exclude them from the centre.

The interior ministry has said 410,000 people marched last Saturday, when a strong police presence mostly prevented a repeat of the widespread violence and looting that swept French cities during a first wave of mass protest on 17 October.

Unions and the gilets jaunes movement protesting over low wages, the cost of living and deteriorating public services have joined school and university students calling for better learning conditions, with a nationwide ​strike called for 5 November.

Government measures to address the students’ demands – including replacing a creaking university admissions platform and providing loans to local authorities for school renovations – did not go far enough, student leaders said.

articles.title: Spain’s trust in high-speed rail ‘broken’ after second deadly crash this year, says PM
articles.summary: Pedro Sánchez vows to investigate crash that killed 69 people – and rebuild public confidence
body: Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has admitted “trust in high-speed rail has been broken” after Wednesday’s train collision that killed at least 69 people, injured more than 100 and prompted a national debate on the safety of the country’s rail network.

Sánchez said Spain was “working tirelessly” to provide information as quickly as possible to the families of the victims – who include people from at least 23 different foreign countries – adding his government was committed to finding what had caused the country’s second deadly train collision this year.

Two trains, one from Spain’s state-owned Renfe and the other from the private rail company Iryo, were travelling from Madrid towards the southern region of Andalucía on Wednesday when they collided just before 9am. After the Iryo train came to a halt, the other train slammed into its rear, knocking several carriages off the track near Urda, in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha.
The crash came nine months after 46 people were killed and dozens injured when two trains – again one from Renfe and one from Iryo – collided on the same line near the town of Adamuz, in Andalucía.

“It’s unacceptable for a country like Spain – which has such a powerful high-speed rail system – to experience two accidents of this nature and magnitude within a single year,” the prime minister said on Friday.

“Therefore, our task isn’t merely to investigate the causes of what occurred, but also to provide solutions to further strengthen our nation’s high-speed rail system. Public trust in the high-speed system has been broken; the government’s responsibility goes beyond diagnosing the causes – it must also offer solutions to ensure that a tragedy of this scale doesn’t happen again.”

Shortly after Sánchez spoke, Spain’s transport minister, Óscar Puente, who is under growing pressure to resign, gave a press conference in which he dismissed calls to step down, promising instead to focus on “providing the Spanish people with solutions” to restore trust.

“My duty now isn’t to talk about whether or not I carry on with my job; it’s to solve the problems, clarify what happened and offer clear explanations,” he said. “The most important thing I can do is offer solutions as best I can. If the investigation shows there were failures of organisation or control, we will act accordingly. And if individuals are found to be responsible, action will be taken.”

Puente once again suggested that responsibility for Wednesday’s crash appeared to lie within the Madrid control centre of Spain’s state infrastructure operator, Adif. He said that in the run-up to the crash, the LZB signalling system – which automatically halts a train if the line ahead is occupied – had gone down, but emphasised that such incidents were not uncommon. Once the system was down, he said, control and decision-making powers reverted to humans, as was the case in other transport sectors.

The minister added that the crash had occurred after an Adif operator ordered the Renfe train to move off at “normal” speed, rather than following the protocols, which stipulate a top speed of 40kph (25mph) so that drivers can see any dangers ahead in good time. According to a preliminary investigation report released on Thursday, the Renfe train was travelling at between 160kph and 200kph when it hit the Iryo train.
The report concluded: “The sequence of malfunctions, instructions, and actions eventually led to the collision, in the absence of the necessary mitigating barriers.”

Puente said the operator in question was a 48-year-old man, with all the relevant up-to-date training and two years of experience in control centres, who had been managing this specific area since February this year. “So, it was a sector he knew well,” the minister added.
Transport unions have pushed back at the government, arguing that current workloads are too demanding to handle safely and asking for more personnel.

“We believe [the minister] is blaming a mere worker who was working under increasingly poor conditions,” Raquel Ayllón, a spokesperson for SCF, Spain’s railway traffic controllers union, told the Associated Press. “Human error isn’t incomprehensible. What is incomprehensible is that the safety system is regularly failing.”

Spain’s conservative People’s party (PP), which is forecast to topple Sánchez’ socialist-led minority coalition government in next month’s snap general election, has repeatedly called for Puente to step down.

The PP’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, said his party was holding Puente and Sánchez “politically responsible” for both rail crashes. “Whoever has failed in their duty to run the transport ministry properly must bear the consequences,” he said. “And the person who appointed them – and kept them in their post – even more so. If they do not resign, we will remove them at the ballot box.”

Ada Colau, the former Barcelona mayor who now leads the leftwing Frente Amplio coalition that is running in the election, also said Puente needed to go. “We’re not going to engage in the triviality of debating whether that resignation should take place today, tomorrow, or the day after,” she said. “It must happen as soon as possible.”
Puente, asked about the possible effect of the latest crash on the election, said he had given the matter “zero thought”.
“I don’t believe anyone would expect me to be thinking about the election campaign at a moment like this,” he told reporters.

articles.title: ‘Amateur morons’: Flávio Bolsonaro’s short-lived ‘president-elect’ claim met with mockery
articles.summary: Brazilian media ridicule defeated candidate over ‘shameful’ absconsion to US and bizarre letter with wrong coat of arms
body: Flávio Bolsonaro had hoped that by Sunday night people would be calling him the next president of Brazil.

Instead, the far-right politician’s decision to flee to the US after losing the election and – for 58 minutes – to declare himself “Brazil’s true president-elect”, has made him a laughing stock, with Brazilian newspapers and commentators raining a barrage of scornful adjectives down on the conquered candidate.

“If it served any purpose at all, Flávio’s foolishness liberated the democratic right from a family of coup-mongers, which for far too long held it hostage to their reckless folly and irremediable disdain for Brazil,” the conservative Estado de São Paulo newspaper thundered on Friday.

Bolsonaro fled to Miami on Tuesday night, 48 hours after being beaten by his leftwing adversary, the incumbent president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, by 4.4m votes. Lula’s victory has been recognised by rightwing leaders from around the world, including El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele and Italy’s Giorgia Meloni, not to mention Bolsonaro’s own party and many key allies.

But on Wednesday after landing in the US, Bolsonaro published an outlandish letter – reportedly produced with the help of ChatGPT – in which he declared himself “the true president-elect of Brazil” and made phoney claims about election fraud.

Perhaps most bizarrely, he claimed he would continue to lead Brazil’s opposition from abroad, comparing himself to Charles de Gaulle, who in the 1940s led a French government-in-exile against the Nazis from London, and the 19th-century Cuban independence hero José Martí, who challenged the Spanish empire from New York.

“They were all treated as criminals by the regimes they confronted. History called them something else,” Bolsonaro said, also likening himself to Venezuela’s Nobel laureate María Corina Machado and Rui Barbosa, a Brazilian politician who went into exile in London in the late 19th century after challenging an authoritarian president known as “the Iron Marshal”.

Just under an hour after Bolsonaro’s proclamation was first published on social media, a corrected version was issued, altering his claimed status to “leader of Brazil” – reportedly after he was upbraided by Trump administration officials keen to avoid a full-blown diplomatic split with Brazil’s actual leaders.

The amended letter also updated the out-of-date Brazilian coat of arms that had been used erroneously in the letterhead of the first version referring to the “United States of Brazil” – a name the South American country has not used since 1967.
Bolsonaro’s flight – and his brief but bogus claim to be “president-elect” of one of the world’s largest democracies – prompted an outpouring of opprobrium and ridicule.
“[This letter] seems to have been written by a foolhardy, loony halfwit,” Flávia Oliveira, a prominent political commentator, told the network GloboNews.

The Estado de São Paulo’s leader writers said: “Flávio’s letter isn’t worth the ink of this newspaper, but there’s no way the embarrassment can be ignored,” before savaging a man they called “a con artist of the highest order”.

The Rio broadsheet O Globo said Bolsonaro’s “shameful and sneaky” decision to abscond laid bare the “pathetic” nature of his political movement, Bolsonarismo, while the Folha de São Paulo said it exposed the true nature of the “authoritarian, ignorant, incompetent” Bolsonaro family.
José Casado, a columnist for the conservative magazine Veja, wrote: “The comedy storyline has already guaranteed him a spot in the pages of political satire.”
Merval Pereira, a conservative columnist for O Globo, called Bolsonaro “a madhouse Napoleon”.

Even Silas Malafaia, a pugnacious televangelist who is close to Bolsonaro’s jailed father, Jair Bolsonaro, had harsh words. “Bolsonaro’s kids are jackasses … A bunch of amateur morons,” Malafaia was quoted as saying by O Globo.

Some observers see Bolsonaro’s post-defeat getaway as proof that his dispirited movement is dead. “I think Bolsonarismo was defeated once and for all,” Lula’s chief foreign policy adviser, Celso Amorim, said this week, calling the result “the last gasp of a radical, irrational, lying right wing”.
Related: Brazil’s victory for the planet and democracy: seven lessons from Lula’s win

The Estado de São Paulo’s editorial board agreed. “Flávio belongs to the past and will soon vanish into the basement of political irrelevance from which he should never have emerged,” they predicted, urging conservatives to ditch Bolsonaro and throw their weight behind his ally Tarcísio de Freitas, the São Paulo governor.
Others warned Bolsonarismo would remain a powerful political force, even if the Bolsonaro family’s leadership of the far-right movement was now in doubt.

Social media users were also merciless in their reaction to Bolsonaro’s short-lived claim to be “president-elect”. One meme invited supporters to attend his January inauguration – at Cinderella Castle in Walt Disney World, Orlando. Another parodied his movement’s fascist-inspired slogan “God, homeland and family”, which became “Goodbye, homeland and family”.

Donald Trump has declined to publicly recognise the result of an election he has called “a very great embarrassment to the people of Brazil”. But a US diplomatic cable obtained by the Folha de São Paulo called Lula’s victory “surprising but definitive”.
Asked if he saw Bolsonaro as Brazil’s “rightful” leader, the US president replied: “I won’t get involved.”

articles.title: Gulf states must rethink trillion-dollar defence in light of US-Iran war, says report
articles.summary: IISS study questions overreliance on American support and ‘overdependence on expensive, high-end systems’
body: Gulf states are going to have to reconfigure their trillion-dollar defences given the damage inflicted on their economies and the questionable continued value of US bases in the face of Iranian attack, according to a study by the International Institute for Strategic Studies.

The report says that in the weeks before the 8 April ceasefire, 12 regional states, overwhelmingly in the Gulf, faced 4,670 Iranian one-way attack drones and more than 1,400 ballistic missiles. Nearly half were aimed at the United Arab Emirates. Although the vast majority were repelled, one estimate of the damage to energy infrastructure cited by the report is put as high as $58bn (£43bn).

Iran would portray either a reduction or complete withdrawal of US forces from the region as “a strategic success and vindication of its steadfastness, but also use it to embarrass the Gulf states about their decades-long courtship of US protection”.

The report says the war also highlights another “uncomfortable truth for the Gulf states: not only has their trillion-dollar acquisition of US weapons not translated into US protection at the crucial time, but their respective militaries are also not adequately prepared for the new kind of attritional air war to which they are being exposed”.

Despite huge investment in mainly US armaments, the report identified significant shortcomings: “overwhelming reliance on US-supplied air- and missile-defence systems and munitions; a failure to achieve regional defence integration; a shortage of minesweeping capability; limited retaliatory options; and the prohibitive costs stemming from an overdependence on expensive, high-end systems to take down relatively inexpensive drones and missiles”.

The report is neutral on whether the divided Gulf states should seek a new non-aggression pact with Iran, but notes that the US-Iran war has shown longstanding defence and security partnerships with the US “have failed to ensure adequate protection against Iranian aggression”.
It adds: “If anything, US military bases and defence partnerships with the US have provided Iran with another pretext for attacks against the Gulf states.”
Public opinion on the US in the Gulf has also been shifting, it says, “from security provider to strategic liability”.

Any reduction or withdrawal of US forces from the Gulf region would be portrayed by Iran “as a strategic success and vindication of its steadfastness” and would also be used “to embarrass the Gulf states about their decades-long courtship of US protection,” the report notes.
Related: Friday briefing: Israel has a dilemma - can its opposition govern with Palestinian parties?

The study comes after Chris Murphy, the Democrat senator and member of the senate foreign relations committee, said a debate was under way in the US military about the value of seeking to rebuild the damaged US bases in the Gulf.

Murphy said the Gulf state leadership “want us to rebuild” and “to keep a presence in the region”, but asked: “What good is it to have a base in the region to protect American interests if within 24 hours of a hot war starting, it is wiped off the map?
“We would be criminally incompetent as stewards of taxpayer dollars if we were to rebuild bases that are blown up within hours of the next war starting.

“So clearly, we are going to have to have a smaller footprint in the region, and the limiting principle on the footprint that we rebuild will be ‘what can we protect?’ because we clearly cannot protect the scope of our footprint today and if we can’t protect it, it is useless.”
Murphy suggested that, at the very least, the US may need to relocate its bases in the eastern Mediterranean further away from Iranian missiles.

articles.title: Beijing Queer film festival cancelled after harassment from authorities
articles.summary: Forums for discussion of feminist and LGBTQ+ views face growing intolerance from Chinese state, say experts
body: Beijing’s annual independent queer film festival has been cancelled after what is understood to have been a campaign of sustained harassment from authorities.
Beijing Queer film festival, which was due to begin on Friday in China’s capital, is one of the country’s oldest independent film festivals.

In a statement posted on Instagram late on Thursday, the organisers said: “We regret to inform you that the Love Queer Film Week … has been cancelled. We sincerely apologise for any inconvenience and disappointment that the cancellation of this event may cause to those who planned to participate or had been looking forward to the film week.”
Police had increased pressure on the festival through repeated phone calls in recent weeks, it is understood.

Founded in 2001 by a group of Peking University students, the festival grew to become the only film festival in mainland China to offer a public forum for films and discussions exploring LGBTQ+ issues.

The Chinese authorities have grown increasingly intolerant of open discussion of feminist or LGBTQ+ issues. Film festivals in particular attract particular scrutiny because they provide an opportunity to platform narratives that sit outside the Communist party’s worldview.

Beijing Independent film festival, China’s most prominent independent film festival, was closed down in 2014 after the authorities detained the founders and shut off the electricity supply to the venue. Last year, an independent Chinese film festival that was due to be held in New York was cancelled after harassment from the Chinese authorities, an incident which raised concern about transnational repression.

Maya Wang, the deputy Asia director for Human Rights Watch, said: “The Chinese government under Xi has been relentlessly tightening social and ideological control, and so any activities outside of those sanctioned by the party-state are subjected to intensifying scrutiny and often also official harassment.

“The authorities have put more pressure on what little is left of China’s civil society, as well as the LGBT communities and independent film-makers. A queer film festival basically faces all of these overlapping pressures.”
Hongwei Bao, a professor of Chinese studies at the University of St Andrews who focuses on LGBT issues, said that the festival was “a beacon for LGBT resilience” in China.
“The shutdown of the Love Queer Cinema Week has a chilling affect on the Chinese queer community,” Bao said.

In June this year, screenings of films with LGBTQ+ themes that were scheduled to be held in Beijing during Pride month at the Institut Français, a French cultural centre, were cancelled because of police harassment.

Despite the increased pressure, Beijing Queer film festival remains a popular event. Several international film-makers whose work had been selected for the festival had travelled to China to participate. Last year, the festival received 200 volunteer applications, four times the number received in 2024.
Beijing’s public security bureau could not be reached for comment.

articles.title: ‘Swift justice’: Student List supporters focus on cleaning up Serbia’s rotten institutions
articles.summary: After improbable election victory, the unconventional grassroots movement says it will prioritise dismissal of corrupt officials
body: In Belgrade’s Pioneers Park, just across from the national assembly, a small crowd craned their necks to listen. One woman held aloft a placard reading “Love prevailed for the people and Serbia”. With a bouquet of media microphones in front of them, members of the Student List, the direct democracy movement that won an improbable but decisive victory in Sunday’s election, gathered under the trees.

Having spent days bathing in the euphoria of their unexpected triumph, the candidates’ focus was now clear: the cleaning up of the rotten institutions that had increasingly blighted the lives of Serbs over the 14 years of government by the populist leader Aleksandar Vučić and his Serbian Progressive party (SNS). They called for the dismissal of many senior law enforcement officials, among them the chiefs of the criminal police, the paramilitary gendarmerie and an anti-terrorism unit.

Student List candidate Svetlana Stanarević was applauded when she accused the officials of violating the law. She also called for the director of Serbia’s internal intelligence agency to resign, accusing him of running the organisation as “a party security service, not a state security service”.

There was approval, too, for the “reopening or expediting of cases” related to the disaster that sparked the student protest movement. Sunday will mark the second anniversary of the canopy collapse that killed 16 people at a renovated railway station in Serbia’s second city, Novi Sad. There have yet to be any convictions.
The announcements on Thursday were the Student List’s way of stressing they intended to put anti-corruption efforts at the heart of government.

“For years, for decades, people have been really frustrated,” said Iva Marković, a Student List candidate and political ecologist who founded the Right to Water initiative. “We see this as a time where everyone who was honestly and credibly working within [public] institutions can do their jobs. They are no longer under political pressure, and we ask them to do their jobs, which also means for prosecutors to prosecute, and police to investigate.”

Reinforcing the student movement’s key principles is also a way, perhaps, to allay concerns that the Student List might not know how to handle its stunning victory over Vučić and the SNS. The movement is not a traditional party. It does not have a hierarchy or leader – and although the students selected the list of candidates, they will not have any direct control over the people who have been elected, once they have been sworn in as MPs.
Marković said the common commitment the students and their parliamentary candidates had made should not be underestimated.

“The process didn’t start with the elections,” she noted, adding that preventing “individualism” from undermining core goals had been key to the student movement’s success. “When you dream together with some people, it’s very hard to forget this dream, even if you are in parliament.”

Borko Stefanović’s choice of a pizzeria themed around ’Allo ’Allo! as a meeting place reflects Serbia’s enthusiasm for British sitcoms of a certain vintage. Only Fools and Horses is a particular favourite, with its tales of thwarted schemes and broken dreams chiming strongly in a country that has been through turbulent times since the early 1990s.

Stefanović knows this better than most. He was part of the political movement opposed to Slobodan Milošević – and saw the democratic coalition that emerged from the overthrow of Serbia’s notorious former president fritter away its early promise. It is not a film he cares to watch a second time.

“There is this almost legendary saying in Serbia that we won on the 5th of October [2000] over Milošević, but we never had the 6th of October,” he said, adding that the Student List was correct to prioritise the dismissal of corrupt officials.

“Get the right people in the right places, bring swift legal justice, liberate institutions and the media, and allow the prosecutor’s office to arrest criminals. Everyone who wants to contribute to the reforms needs to get on board and to do everything we can to make this excellent example in Europe a lasting one.”

Perched on a sofa in a coffee roastery in Belgrade’s old town, Tara Blagojević was convinced the movement she has been a part of already had the right people in place. With the elections over, she said it was down to the successful candidates to form a government. The student assemblies will take a less active role, acting as “advisers or kind of supervisors”.

“Everything’s going to be fine,” Blagojević insisted, adding that although the Student List was “kind of a political experiment”, the people who will soon be sworn in as MPs “recognise each other’s strengths and are able to project who can be suitable to do certain things within the new government”.
Related: How students toppled Serbia’s strongman – podcast

Slobodan Tomić is optimistic about the Student List’s prospects. The Belgrade-born political scientist at the University of York has been following the student movement since its inception. “It is an extraordinary change,” he said of the party’s unconventional structure. “I couldn’t find any example across the world of anything similar happening.
“The MPs had to sign a pledge that they would follow through the programme that the Student List had created. So on paper, there isn’t much space for drift.”

The organisers of the famous Exit music festival are also convinced. They moved the event out of the country this year in protest at the policies of Vučić and the SNS. They confirmed that Exit would return to its home in Novi Sad next year.

The news further energised the crowd at Belgrade’s first big gig since the election, where the euphoria showed no sign of subsiding. Chants of “Victory!” welcomed Fontaines DC on stage among the shipping containers at the port of Belgrade. “Congratulations,” responded the Irish singer Grian Chatten. “This is your moment, not ours.”

A former punk rock bassist himself, Stefanović is sure that assessment is correct. “These wonderful, wonderful people from the Student List and the student movement, they know exactly what needs to be done,” he said. He added just one caveat from experience: “Don’t blow it.”

articles.title: Houthis sending Taiz ‘back to the stone age’, governor of besieged Yemen city says
articles.summary: Oxygen, food and water supplies running low and massacres taking place, says Nabil Shamsan
body: The Houthis are trying to send the city of Taiz back to the stone age, the city’s governor said in a briefing designed to urge the international community to do more to lift the month-long siege.

Nabil Shamsan said massacres were taking place in Yemen’s third city, that oxygen and water supplies were running out and that rubbish was piling up in the streets due to landfill sites being either full or inaccessible.

The city’s daily minimum water needs are estimated at about 35,000 cubic metres, he said, but no more than 1,000 cubic metres was being allowed to reach it each day and that water shipments were being stopped at Houthi roadblocks surrounding the city.
With food stocks depleted and the price of wheat soaring, he said “citizens are heading back to the stone age”. Restaurants had closed due to the lack of fuel.

Shamsan said that as many as 1,800 people were in need of dialysis treatment but were unable to access supplies, that 120 health centres had been suspended and schools had closed, affecting hundreds of thousands of children.

He said 64 people had been killed, including civilians, from August to 20 October 2026 and a further 173 injured. More than 6,400 newly displaced families, each averaging seven members, had come to the city to flee the fighting.
“We are not talking about living, just surviving,” he said.

His account contradicted one given by the Houthi leader, Abdul-Malik Badr al-Din al-Houthi, who said: “The way is open for food, medicine, and humanitarian aid to enter the city and even for Saudi-backed groups to do so. Anyone who wants to verify that there is no siege on the city of Taiz can go to the city and see.”
Shamsan said that Houthis forces had a near-total grip on the roads into the city, adding the group had issued a choice to the more than 800,000 inside the city “either to leave or to die”.

He accused the Houthis of not waging a military battle but a battle to change the identity of Yemen, with captured villages being taken over by new religious leaders with education and religious curricula being changed. “This is not a military war but a war of vengeance,” he said.

People in occupied territories were being required to show loyalty to the Zaydi religion and to sign forms affirming they had joined the Houthis. “They are not starting a war but an revolution in identity,” Shamsan said, adding that scores of children from each village were being forcibly ordered without their parents’ consent to join the frontlines in Saada and elsewhere.

Vowing the people of Taiz would resist until the end, he said statements of solidarity were of no use and that what was needed was access for aid agencies, including the UN, to deliver supplies to the city.

Shamsan was reluctant to divulge details of the state of the military campaign, but said shelling of the city was becoming more frequent and that communication between the city and rural areas had broken down. Houthis now controlled the mobile networks and were sending messages to citizens to end their resistance, while eavesdropping on all conversations, he said. Mobile networks were “completely disrupted”, he said, adding that he was speaking only 2-5km from the frontlines.

Most independent agencies agree that life inside the city is rapidly deteriorating. Niku Jafarnia, a Yemen researcher at Human Rights Watch, said: “Renewed efforts by the Houthis to cut off food, water, and medicine to Taiz show their utter disregard for civilian lives.
“Throughout the 12-year-long siege of Taiz, the Houthis have bombed, starved and denied humanitarian aid to a million residents of the city with scant adherence to international law.”

articles.title: Friday briefing: Israel has a dilemma - can its opposition govern with Palestinian parties?
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: Benjamin Netanyahu has been left without a majority, now it is up to the coalition to find out whether the desire for change will prove to be a defining political moment
body: Good morning. It was described by many Israelis as the most consequential election in their country’s history. And, as the final votes were tallied, it has delivered a result that presents Israel with a significant dilemma.

Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition has lost its mandate while the opposition has a clear majority: but only if the Jewish Israeli opposition bloc, led by retired general Gadi Eisenkot, is prepared to make a governing pact with Palestinian Israeli parties, which have secured a historic result.

But the country that is desperate for change remains bitterly divided. After a campaign mired in racism, during which Israel’s far-right demonised the Palestinian population as the enemy within, Netanyahu has gone further since Tuesday’s vote, claiming that Palestinian-led parties have “stolen the election”, despite Israeli authorities insisting there is no evidence of election fraud.
As coalition talks commence, I spoke to our chief Middle East correspondent Emma Graham-Harrison in Tel Aviv, about false narratives and the stark choice facing the country. But first, the headlines.

UK politics | John Healey has backed away from cutting the cost of welfare this parliament, amid dire warnings his first budget could lead to brutal spending cuts because of a £28bn shortfall in public finances.

Patrick Stewart | The acclaimed British stage and screen actor renowned for both Shakespeare and sci-fi, died at his home in Los Angeles after “a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia”, his longtime spokesperson said.
Environment | One of the most ambitious nature recovery projects ever undertaken in England can go ahead after campaigners announced they had raised £30m to buy an estate in Northumberland.

Europe | Spain began three days of mourning on Thursday for at least 69 people who died in a high-speed rail collision, as hospitals continued to treat dozens of injured passengers and train drivers went on strike to urge more investment in railway safety.

US news | The Trump administration has opened a criminal investigation in California over claims that thousands of noncitizens are registered to vote in the state, and has begun subpoenaing election officials.

With the final results released early on Friday local time, Netanyahu’s bloc won 53 seats, compared with 48 for the grouping led by rival Eisenkot. Palestinian parties won 19 seats, a record high. No single party has ever claimed a majority of 61 seats, so Israel has always been governed by coalitions.

With neither bloc reaching the 61 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset, Israeli president Isaac Herzog is expected to invite the party most likely to be able to form a government to start coalition negotiations, and has already urged politicians to have an “open mind” before talks begin. The country potentially faces weeks of rancour and uncertainty.

Yair Golan, the leader of the centre-left Democrats, a junior partner in the Jewish Israeli opposition bloc, told Israeli media on Thursday that he was meeting Eisenkot and others for initial talks. If the opposition can’t agree some kind of coalition, or even secure Palestinian support for a minority government, Netanyahu may have a lifeline. He is already pushing for a right-wing governing coalition, and would probably welcome new elections or a lengthy period of uncertainty during which he will stay on as caretaker prime minister.
And yet throughout the campaign, voters’ discontent with Netanyahu was evident.

That didn’t mean a shift to the left: young Israelis are more rightwing than older generations, as Emma wrote about here. The national conversation ahead of the election was dominated by security at home and abroad. Although he was in charge on 7 October 2023, when Hamas attacks resulted in the deaths of about 1,200 people, the majority of them civilians, the prime minister tried to shift blame on to the security services.

His opponents pledged a state commission of inquiry into the events of 7 October, and spoke to voters’ concerns about the social toll of three years of multi-front wars, and anger about the draft exemption for ultra-orthodox young men when other Israelis are spending hundreds of days on reserve duty.

Throughout the campaign, Netanyahu and his far-right allies have framed Palestinian voters – who make up about 20% of the population – as a direct threat to ​the state, with Netanyahu repeating the slogan “the right or Palestine”, which rhymes in Hebrew.
“It’s both tragic and depressing,” Emma tells me, “attempting to paint Palestinians as untrustworthy citizens with dual loyalties, a racist trope that also appears in antisemitic attacks.”

This tactic extended to election day, when voters received a robocall purporting to come from the prime minister falsely claiming that Palestinian party leaders had been caught with envelopes full of cash. Netanyahu and his allies repeatedly made claims about high turnout in Palestinian areas, in a bid to get his own voters out.

Then on Wednesday night, Netanyahu reacted to the high Palestinian turnout and success of Arab Israeli parties by claiming, again without providing evidence, they had “stolen the election,” calling for the central elections committee and Shin Bet internal security agency to investigate foreign interference in the vote. These claims were amplified by far-right Israeli finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, who called for the arrest of Arab Israeli leaders.

He was swiftly accused of using smear tactics to cling to power. Eisenkot warned that Likud and Netanyahu “have embarked on a coordinated, organised campaign seeking to delegitimise the results of the election”. President Herzog stepped in with a rebuke to the prime minister and said “we must avoid tarnishing an entire community”. Meanwhile, Qatar’s foreign ministry spokesperson rejected “ridiculous and dangerous” accusations his country had interfered in Tuesday’s election.
It bears repeating: Israeli police and the central elections committee have said there is no evidence of election fraud.
The Palestinian-led parties who could be kingmakers
There was a surge in support for Arab parties after Palestinian citizens came out in historic numbers to vote.

Many had boycotted previous elections “on the grounds that participating endorses a discriminatory system or because they felt their representatives had little leverage”, Emma explains. But this year, the mood changed: “They’re watching ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, a genocidal war in Gaza, and are under huge pressure inside Israel from an openly racist government, which has allowed organised crime to soar, ramped up home demolitions, and targeted political speech. They felt that, if Netanyahu managed to get another mandate with his far right allies including [extremist security minister] Ben-Gvir, this would only accelerate.”

The Joint List – which represents a number of mainly leftist Israeli Arab-led parties – is led by Yousef Jabareen. He has previously said the Joint ​List could not join an Eisenkot-led government because of its support for Israel’s ‌military operation in Gaza and southern Lebanon, but has left open the possibility of bolstering a minority government through confidence votes.

The other main Palestinian party, Ra’am, is led by Mansour Abbas, and includes a Jewish former chief of police as number two on their slate, a signal of their commitment to working with Jewish Israelis but also their desire to tackle organised crime, which is a big issue for the Palestinian population.

Ra’am joined Naftali Bennett’s government in 2021, the first time a Palestinian party entered an Israeli coalition, but their pact collapsed after 18 months, partly because of disagreements over the occupied West Bank.
A survey taken as polls closed on Tuesday showed that a clear majority of opposition voters supported forming a government with Ra’am in order to unseat Netanyahu.

While Eisenkot has not ruled out cooperating with Palestinians because of their race, he has effectively barred them from a future coalition by laying out conditions for any partner which are politically impossible for them to accept.

Still, Emma notes an inconsistency: Palestinian citizens play a key role in Israeli life, with outsized representation in professions from medics to security guards, including much of the team at Eisenkot’s election night HQ. “You would think some of these parties might ask, if you trust Palestinian citizens to secure your campaign events why don’t you trust them to be part of your government?”

Emma points to a rarely referenced precedent from three decades ago, when Yitzhak Rabin relied on Palestinian support for a minority government as he sought a negotiated end to the Israel-Palestine conflict. Might such a compromise be possible now?

“This whole campaign has been based on Israeli voters urgently wanting change, because Netanyahu has led them to the brink of disaster. And now they have voted, this is an existential moment,” she said

“You have a parliamentary majority to bring about that change. Is your racism ultimately more important to you? What matters more: the desire to exclude Palestinians or the desire to get rid of Netanyahu?”

“Netanyahu accused of smearing Arab voters to hold on to power”, is the Guardian’s front page today.

The Times leads with “Defence to benefit from off-the-book spending”, the Telegraph writes “Prepare for decade of pain, warn IFS”, and the i Paper leads on “No welfare cuts before election – as Britons face ‘worst decade’ for pay growth”, while the Mail has “Humiliation for Healey”.
The FT says “Alphabet shares battered as cash burn deepens investor fears over AI returns”. Metro writes “Manosphere ‘as bad as smoking’” and the Sun splashes “Fright of the round table”.
Shock and anger in Spain after deadly train crash

Spain has begun three days of mourning after at least 69 people were killed and more than 100 were injured in a crash between two high-speed trains. The town of Urda has become the site of a major operation, as emergency services continue to search through the wreckage and relatives wait for news of their loved ones. There is growing public anger over the incident, which is the second fatal train collision in Spain in less than a year. Lucy Hough speaks to the Guardian’s Madrid correspondent, Sam Jones.
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

Moving away from diesel-powered ferries to electric vessels has not been an easy task. Batteries are heavy, which means more power is needed to propel electric boats forward through significant resistance. But more companies are finding solutions to the problem and creating workable vessels that reduce emissions.

One such company is Vessev, whose electric ferries rely on underwater wings called hydrofoils that lift the boat above the water. This dramatically reduces drag by up to 66%, making their boats more energy-efficient. Swedish company Candela are designing boats, they claim, which can reduce energy use by 80% compared with conventional vessels of a similar type. “I think in a more sustainable future we’re likely to see more and more vessels like this around the world,” Eric Laakmann, the chief executive and co-founder of Vessev, said.
